title: Electrical Continuity Testing
summary: What continuity means, how a multimeter or test lamp is used to find breaks, how to read results, common faults, and safe working.

p: Electrical continuity means an unbroken path for current in a circuit. A conductor is continuous if it forms a complete path from one terminal to the other. A break in the path (a cut wire, a blown fuse, a faulty switch) is called a discontinuity and stops the current.
Continuity testing is a way of checking whether there is a complete path for current in a circuit or component.

It is based on Ohm's law, V = IR. A low or zero resistance means a complete (closed) path. A very high or infinite resistance means an open circuit (a break). In continuity mode a multimeter sends a tiny current through the part and sees whether it can come back.

Digital multimeter: the most reliable; in continuity mode it beeps when there is continuity; it can also measure resistance. Analogue multimeter: a needle deflects for low resistance; no deflection means no continuity. Continuity tester: a simple hand tool with a battery and a bulb or buzzer. Test lamp: a bulb, a battery and two leads; it lights if there is a complete path.

Safety first: switch off the power and unplug the device before testing, because a continuity test must never be done on a live circuit. Steps: 1. Set the meter to continuity mode (or to the lowest ohm range). 2. Put the black probe in the COM socket and the red probe in the socket marked Ω (or VΩ). 3. Touch the two probes together; the meter should beep, to show it is working. 4. Touch the probes to the two ends of the wire or component. 5. Watch the reading or listen for the beep.

p: Checking wiring in homes and offices; car repairs (wiring, sensors); quality control for circuit boards; finding faults in old installations; industrial control panels; aircraft and rail safety checks; checking connections before powering a new instrument.

Never test a live circuit. Discharge capacitors first. Choose the right range. Check probes for damage. Work with dry hands, on a dry floor and with rubber-soled shoes. Label tested wires. Keep flammable things away.

A resistor of 1.5 Ω shows 1.5 on the meter. Does this show continuity? Yes: the resistance is low, so a path exists. Exam answers: continuity testing is used to detect open circuits (B). A good conductor shows a beep (C).

Switch tested, no beep: the contacts may be dirty, worn or broken, or the switch might be in the open position. Remedy: switch it to the closed position and test again; clean or replace the switch if there is still no beep.

Testing a car's headlamp wiring: disconnect the battery; take out the bulb; test the live wire from the switch to the bulb socket, then the earth path to the body; check the fuse and the switch; repair any break; reconnect.

sections.h: Test lamp for a broken wire
p: Connect the lamp and battery in series with the wire. If the lamp lights, the wire is unbroken. If it does not, there is a break somewhere. Test the wire section by section to find where.

title: Electroplating
summary: How electroplating works by electrolysis, the parts, the reactions at the electrodes, conditions, metals used, uses, limits and safety.

p: Electroplating is putting a thin layer of one metal on the surface of another object by passing an electric current through an electrolyte. It is used for protection, decoration and to improve conduction.

It is a form of electrolysis. A direct current (d.c.) passes through an electrolyte containing ions of the plating metal. The metal to be deposited is the anode (+). The object to be coated is the cathode (–). Positive metal ions in the solution are attracted to the cathode, gain electrons (are reduced) and form a coating. If the anode is made of the plating metal, it dissolves to replace the ions used.

img.alt: A beaker of copper sulfate with a key and battery; the cathode (object to be plated) on the left, a copper anode on the right, copper ions and sulfate ions in the solution and anode mud at the bottom
img.cap: Copper plating: the object (Me) is the cathode; the copper anode dissolves.

rows: Gives the direct current that drives the process

p: Electrolyte: copper(II) sulfate solution. Anode: copper plate. Cathode: the iron or steel spoon.
At the cathode (–): Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu(s). Copper ions are reduced and deposit as copper on the spoon.
At the anode (+): Cu(s) → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻. The copper anode dissolves and replaces the ions in the solution.

The thickness depends on the current, time, concentration and temperature. By Faraday's first law the mass deposited is m = Zit, where Z is the electrochemical equivalent (about 3.3 × 10⁻⁷ kg/C for copper), I is the current and t the time in seconds. For example, 2 A for 30 minutes (1,800 s) deposits about 3.3 × 10⁻⁷ × 2 × 1,800 = 1.2 × 10⁻³ kg, or about 1.2 g, of copper.
A clean surface; a steady d.c. supply; the correct concentration of electrolyte; a moderately warm solution; the right position of the electrodes; and enough time for the thickness wanted.
Study the table.

head: Plating metal
Reason
rows: Resists corrosion and gives a shine
Decoration, and good conduction in electronics
Base layer for other platings; appearance

p: Gold or silver jewellery; car parts (bumpers, handles); cutlery and kitchenware; electrical connectors and circuit boards; coins and medals; protective coatings on tools and machines; galvanised iron (zinc-plated) to prevent rust.

Advantages: it improves appearance; prevents corrosion; improves conduction; makes the surface harder and longer lasting; reduces friction in machine parts; makes cheaper metals look valuable. Disadvantages: it is costly when gold or silver is used; the chemicals can pollute the environment if not managed; the layer can wear off; it needs controlled conditions; poor cleaning makes the coating stick badly.

Wear gloves and goggles. Work in a well-ventilated place. Avoid skin contact with the electrolyte. Do not let the electrodes touch in the beaker (that makes a short circuit). Wash your hands and equipment afterwards. Label and store chemicals safely. Dispose of used solutions responsibly, not down a drain.

The object to be plated is joined to the negative terminal (B). Electroplating involves electrolysis (C). Experiment to zinc-plate an iron nail: clean the nail with sandpaper and rinse; join it to the negative terminal of a d.c. supply as the cathode; use a zinc plate as the anode, joined to the positive terminal; put both in a beaker of zinc sulfate solution without touching; switch on and leave for some time; remove the nail, rinse and dry it, and see the grey zinc layer. Chromium plating of car parts is done by cleaning, plating first with copper and nickel layers, and then a thin layer of chromium; zinc coating protects steel bridges by galvanising, because the zinc corrodes first (it is more reactive) and so protects the steel.

title: Applications of Electromagnetic Fields (1): Induction, Eddy Currents, Generators and Motors
summary: Faraday's and Lenz's laws, eddy currents, mutual inductance, the a.c. generator, motors, transformers, loudspeakers and relays.

p: Faraday's law: when the magnetic flux linked with a circuit changes, an e.m.f. is induced in it. Its size is proportional to the rate of change of flux linkage. Lenz's law: the induced e.m.f. is in a direction that opposes the change or motion producing it.

Eddy currents are loops of current induced in a piece of metal by a changing magnetic field. They flow in closed loops in planes at right angles to the field, in a direction that opposes the motion of the conductor in the field. They waste energy as heat in transformer cores (which are laminated, made of thin insulated sheets, to cut them down) but are useful in induction heating and magnetic braking.
Mutual inductance is the production of an induced current or voltage in one coil by a changing current in a neighbouring coil.

A coil is turned in a magnetic field. As it turns, the flux through it changes, and an e.m.f. is induced in it. (The note says the e.m.f. is 'reduced'; the correct word is induced.) The ends of the coil are joined to two slip rings, which turn with the coil, and carbon brushes touch the rings and lead the current to the load. The slip rings give an alternating voltage. The direction of the induced current is found by Fleming's right-hand rule.

img.alt: A simple a.c. generator with a coil rotating between the N and S poles of a magnet, slip rings on the shaft and wires to a load

sections.h: What decides the size of the induced e.m.f.?
p: The speed of rotation of the coil, the cross-sectional area of the coil, the number of turns in the coil, and the strength of the magnetic field (flux density).

A motor changes electrical energy into mechanical energy. When current flows in a coil in a magnetic field, a force acts on the coil and makes it turn (Fleming's left-hand rule). Two things decide the direction of rotation: the direction of the current and the direction of the magnetic field. Reversing either one reverses the direction of rotation.
Generator: changes mechanical energy to electrical energy by induction (Fleming's right-hand rule).

Transformer: moves electrical energy from one circuit to another by mutual induction. It has a primary and a secondary coil on a soft-iron core. A changing current in the primary induces a voltage in the secondary: V_s ÷ V_p = N_s ÷ N_p. A step-up transformer has more turns on the secondary and raises the voltage; a step-down transformer has fewer. It works only with a.c. Used in phone chargers and in the power grid.
Loudspeaker: an alternating current in a coil attached to a diaphragm makes the coil move in the field of a permanent magnet, and the diaphragm produces sound.

An electromagnetic relay is a switch worked by an electromagnet: a small current in the coil pulls a contact to switch a large current in another circuit. An electric bell works when the electromagnet pulls the armature, which breaks the contact and switches the magnet off; the armature springs back, makes contact again, and the action repeats to ring the bell.

title: Applications of Electromagnetic Fields (2): MRI, Induction Heating, Wireless Power and Risks
summary: Everyday and technological uses of electromagnetic fields, advantages and risks, and answers to the past-question tasks.

p: Electric power transmission (transformers and high-voltage lines use alternating fields). Household appliances (microwave ovens use microwaves, induction cookers use induced currents). Communication (radio, television, phones and Wi-Fi use electromagnetic waves). Medical equipment (MRI scanners and diathermy). Security (metal detectors, RFID tags, airport scanners).

A patient lies inside a very strong magnet. The field makes the hydrogen nuclei in the body line up. Pulses of radio waves knock them out of line; as they return, they give out signals that a computer builds into detailed pictures of soft tissues such as the brain, muscles and organs. It does not use X-rays.

A coil carrying a high-frequency alternating current makes a changing magnetic field. This induces eddy currents in a metal object near it, and the resistance of the metal turns them into heat. Used in metal treatment and induction cookers (which heat the pot, not the cooker top).
Energy is passed between two coils by a changing magnetic field (resonant inductive coupling), without wires. It is used for wireless phone chargers, electric toothbrushes and some electric vehicles.
Non-contact control of devices. Wireless communication. Efficient energy conversion in motors and generators. High-speed non-contact transport (maglev trains). Medical imaging without surgery.

Strong fields can disturb pacemakers and sensitive electronics. High-intensity ionising radiation such as X-rays can be harmful. Electromagnetic interference (EMI) can upset critical systems such as aircraft instruments. Some people worry about long-term exposure to high-frequency fields near phone masts; scientific evidence on this has not shown clear harm at the low levels allowed by safety limits, but research continues. Mitigation: exposure limits, shielding, keeping a distance, and switching devices off when asked to (for example on an aircraft).

Motor: a current-carrying coil in a magnetic field feels a force and turns; the direction depends on the directions of the current and the field. Electromagnetic induction: producing an e.m.f. in a conductor by changing the magnetic flux through it; two uses: generators and transformers.
Two appliances using electromagnetic fields: a microwave oven (microwaves make water molecules vibrate, heating the food) and an electric bell or relay (an electromagnet moves an armature).

title: Models of the Atom (1): Democritus, Dalton, Thomson and Rutherford
summary: The early ideas about the atom and the experiments that changed them, with the strengths and limits of each model.

p: Democritus (about 400 BC) said that matter is made of tiny, indivisible particles he called 'atomos' (meaning uncuttable). It was only philosophy; he had no experiments to prove it.

sections.h: The five models at a glance
p: The picture below shows the five models from the lesson note in order.
(The note gives Thomson's date as 1904 in the picture but 1897 in the text. 1897 is when he discovered the electron by cathode-ray experiments; he proposed the plum-pudding model in 1904.)

img.alt: Five atomic models side by side: Dalton's solid sphere 1803, Thomson's plum pudding 1904, Rutherford's nuclear model 1911, Bohr's planetary model 1913 and the Schrodinger quantum model 1926
img.cap: The development of the atomic model.

p: John Dalton pictured the atom as an indivisible solid sphere. Postulates: all matter is made of indivisible atoms; atoms of the same element are identical in mass and properties; atoms combine in simple whole-number ratios to form compounds; a chemical reaction is a rearrangement of atoms.

Strengths: the first scientific model based on experiments; it explains the conservation of mass and the law of definite proportions. Limitations: no sub-atomic particles (electrons, protons, neutrons); could not explain isotopes (atoms of the same element with different masses) or chemical bonding. (Atoms can in fact be divided.)

J.J. Thomson used a cathode-ray tube and found that cathode rays are negatively charged particles (electrons), deflected by electric and magnetic fields. His model: the atom is a positively charged sphere with electrons embedded in it like raisins in a pudding.
Strengths: it introduced sub-atomic particles and explained electrical conduction. Limitations: no nucleus; could not explain the stability of atoms or the lines in atomic spectra.

Rutherford's team fired alpha particles at a thin gold foil. Observations: most went straight through; a few were deflected; a very few bounced back. Conclusions: the atom is mostly empty space; it has a small, dense, positively charged nucleus; the electrons are outside it.

Strengths: it introduced the nuclear structure of the atom and explained alpha scattering. Limitations: according to classical physics, orbiting electrons should lose energy and spiral into the nucleus, so it could not explain why atoms are stable, and it could not explain the line spectra.

title: Models of the Atom (2): Bohr and Quantum Mechanical Models
summary: Bohr's energy levels and quantised angular momentum, the quantum mechanical model with orbitals, de Broglie wavelength and the uncertainty principle, and a comparison of all models.

p: Niels Bohr improved on Rutherford's model using quantum theory. Postulates: electrons travel in fixed circular orbits (energy levels or shells); they do not radiate energy while in an orbit; they emit or absorb energy only when they jump from one orbit to another.
The energy of level n in hydrogen is Eₙ = –13.6 ÷ n² eV, where n = 1, 2, 3 … is the principal quantum number. Angular momentum is quantised: mvr = nh ÷ 2π.

Successes: it explained the discrete lines in the hydrogen spectrum. Limitations: it works well only for hydrogen and one-electron ions; it could not explain the Zeeman and Stark effects (splitting of lines in magnetic and electric fields); it ignored the wave nature of the electron.

sections.h: Quantum mechanical (Schrödinger) model (1926 to the present)
p: Schrödinger, Heisenberg, de Broglie and Dirac developed it. Electrons are not in fixed orbits but in orbitals, which are regions where an electron is likely to be (probability clouds). Electrons are described by wave functions ψ(x, t). The Heisenberg uncertainty principle: it is impossible to know both the exact position and the exact momentum of an electron at the same time. The de Broglie wavelength is λ = h ÷ p = h ÷ mv.
Strengths: it works for all atoms, including many-electron atoms, and underlies quantum chemistry. Limitations: it is highly mathematical and hard to picture.
Study the table.

head: Model
Scientist

rows: A dense nucleus with orbiting electrons

p: Chemistry (bonding and reactions); spectroscopy (emission and absorption lines); electronics (semiconductors and transistors); medical imaging (MRI and PET); nuclear physics (fission and fusion); quantum computing (control of quantum states); lasers (electron transitions).
Quantised orbits: Bohr's model (B). The discovery of the electron led to the plum-pudding model (A). Orbitals and probability clouds: the quantum mechanical model (C).

Bohr compared with Schrödinger: Bohr has fixed, circular, definite orbits; Schrödinger has probability regions (orbitals). Bohr treats the electron as a particle; Schrödinger treats it as a wave. Bohr works for hydrogen; Schrödinger works for all atoms.

Heisenberg's contribution: the uncertainty principle showed that there is a limit to how precisely certain pairs of quantities can be known at the same time, which means that quantum physics deals with probabilities. Electron orbitals and computer chips: the understanding of electron energy levels and bands in silicon led to semiconductors, diodes and transistors, which make up computer chips.
